title: Activity Selection Problem
description: How **greedy scheduling** picks the maximum number of non-overlapping activities -- and why "earliest finish first" beats the more intuitive "earliest start first".

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Given a set of activities, each with a start and finish time, and only one can run at a time -- select the **maximum number of non-overlapping activities**.

You're a conference organizer with one room and a stack of session requests. Which do you accept? The greedy answer: **always pick the session that ends earliest** -- it leaves the most remaining time for everything else.

This is a textbook case of local greedy decisions producing a **globally optimal** result. It's counterintuitive -- "earliest start" feels right -- but earliest finish is what's provably optimal.

sections.title: Why This Problem Matters
sections.content:
Classrooms, runways, meeting rooms, CPU cores -- none of them can run two overlapping tasks at once. Bad scheduling means idle resources; good scheduling maximizes what actually gets used.

A lecture hall wants the most classes scheduled without overlap. A runway wants max takeoff/landing slots. A single-core CPU wants max completed jobs. Activity Selection models exactly this, with a solution that's both fast and simple.

sections.title: Problem Setup
sections.content:
Each activity has a start and finish time (start < finish). Goal: the largest possible subset where no two overlap.

**Compatible** means one finishes before or exactly when the other starts (A1: 1-4 and A4: 5-7 are compatible, since 4 ≤ 5).

Example set: A1 (1,4), A2 (3,5), A3 (0,6), A4 (5,7), A5 (8,9). The goal: pick the maximum count of mutually compatible activities from this set.

sections.title: Understanding Overlapping Activities
sections.content:
Two intervals overlap unless one ends before or exactly when the other starts.

With A1 (1-4) selected: A2 (3-5) conflicts (starts at 3, before A1 ends at 4). A3 (0-6) conflicts too (spans across A1 entirely). A4 (5-7) is compatible (5 ≥ 4). A5 (8-9) is compatible with A4 (8 ≥ 7).

Pick a long activity early and you block a lot of what comes after. Pick a short, early-finishing one and you keep your options open -- the core intuition behind earliest-finish-first.

sections.title: Core Greedy Idea
sections.content:
Rule: **always select the remaining activity that finishes earliest.**

1. Sort all activities by finish time, ascending.
2. Select the first one (earliest finish).
3. For each next activity, if its start ≥ the last selected activity's finish, select it too.
4. Otherwise skip (it overlaps).

Why not earliest *start*? Activity X (1-100) starts early but runs forever, blocking everything else. Activity Y (2-3) starts a bit later but frees up the room almost immediately. Picking Y preserves far more room for future activities -- that's the whole game.

sections.title: Why Earliest Finishing Works
sections.content:
This satisfies the **Greedy Choice Property**: there's always an optimal solution that includes the earliest-finishing activity.

Proof sketch: take any optimal solution. If its first activity isn't the earliest-finishing one, swap it in -- since the earliest-finishing activity ends no later, this swap can't create a new conflict, and the total count stays the same.

Once that activity's selected, remove everything it conflicts with -- what's left is the exact same kind of problem, just smaller. Apply the same greedy choice again. That's why it works correctly all the way through.

sections.title: Step-by-Step Execution Example
sections.content:
Activities: A1 (1,4), A2 (3,5), A3 (0,6), A4 (5,7), A5 (8,9).

**Sorted by finish:** same order already. `last_finish = -1`, `selected = []`.

* A1 (1,4): 1 ≥ -1? Yes → select. `last_finish = 4`.
* A2 (3,5): 3 ≥ 4? No → skip.
* A3 (0,6): 0 ≥ 4? No → skip.
* A4 (5,7): 5 ≥ 4? Yes → select. `last_finish = 7`.
* A5 (8,9): 8 ≥ 7? Yes → select. `last_finish = 9`.

**Result: A1, A4, A5 -- 3 activities.** Picking by earliest *start* instead would have grabbed A3 first and ended with just 1.

sections.title: Python Implementation
sections.content: Sort by finish time, then track `last_finish` -- select any activity whose start is ≥ that value, and update it each time you do.

codeSnippets.title: Activity Selection implementation
codeSnippets.code:
activities = [
    (1, 4),
    (3, 5),
    (0, 6),
    (5, 7),
    (8, 9)
]

activities.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])

selected = []
last_finish = -1

for start, finish in activities:
    if start >= last_finish:
        selected.append((start, finish))
        last_finish = finish

print(selected)

codeSnippets.title: Count compatible activities
codeSnippets.code:
activities = [(1, 3), (2, 5), (4, 6), (6, 8)]

activities.sort(key=lambda x: x[1])

count = 0
last_finish = -1

for start, finish in activities:
    if start >= last_finish:
        count += 1
        last_finish = finish

print(count)

sections.title: Complexity Analysis
sections.content:
**Sorting:** O(n log n) -- dominates the runtime. **Selection:** one linear pass after sorting, O(n). **Total: O(n log n)**.

**Space:** O(1) for count-only; O(k) to store the k selected activities (k ≤ n).

Brute force checking all 2ⁿ subsets for conflicts would be O(2^n) -- infeasible past small n. Greedy is exponentially faster.

chart.title: Activity Selection complexity
chart.description: Sorting dominates the runtime; compatibility checking is a single linear pass afterward.

sections.title: Why This Problem Is Greedy
sections.content:
Satisfies both properties a greedy algorithm needs:

**Greedy Choice Property:** there's always an optimal solution containing the earliest-finishing activity -- swap it in for whatever else was first, no conflicts introduced.

**Optimal Substructure:** after removing that activity and everything it conflicts with, what's left is a smaller instance of the exact same problem.

Earliest finish never costs you future flexibility -- any other choice finishes at least as late, leaving equal or less room. Not every scheduling problem has this property; Activity Selection does.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
**CPU scheduling** (Shortest Job First, Earliest Deadline First) uses the same greedy logic. **Classroom/runway/room booking systems** maximize slots scheduled per day. **Manufacturing** maximizes jobs completed on a single machine. **Broadcast recording** maximizes shows captured on one channel.

Extensions exist -- weighted activities need Dynamic Programming, multiple rooms need different algorithms entirely -- but for maximizing plain count on one resource, this greedy algorithm is fast, optimal, and simple.

subsections.title: Mistake: Selecting earliest starting activities
subsections.content: An early-starting but long activity can block many others. The right greedy choice is earliest *finish*, not earliest start.

subsections.title: Mistake: Ignoring sorting
subsections.content: This greedy strategy depends entirely on finish-time order. Skip the sort and it won't find the optimal answer.

subsections.title: Mistake: Incorrect overlap checking
subsections.content: Use `current.start >= last_finish` (not strict `>`) so back-to-back activities that start exactly when the last one ends are still allowed.
